tier_reason: Upgraded from D: the peer-reviewed PLDI 2017 paper (Henriksen et al., PDF checked into diku-dk/futhark-website publications/pldi17.pdf) reports Table 1 runtimes and Figure 13 speedups against hand-written OpenCL/CUDA references from Rodinia 3.1, Parboil and FinPar on an NVIDIA GTX 780 Ti (CUDA 8.0) and an AMD FirePro W8100, and the public artifact repo diku-dk/futhark-pldi17 (Makefile, Rodinia instrumentation patch, paper_data/aux_runtimes matching the W8100 column) reproduces it. Not A: host compiler versions, flags, OpenCL driver versions and host CPU are not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PLDI 2017 paper: from about 0.6x (slower, FinPar LocVolCalib on AMD W8100) to 16x (Rodinia NN on GTX 780 Ti) against hand-written OpenCL/CUDA reference implementations; geometric mean 1.81x over the 12 benchmarks that have a low-level CUDA/OpenCL implementation; Futhark slower on 4 of those 12 (geometric mean 0.79x on them). Table 1 runtimes on GTX 780 Ti, reference vs Futhark in ms: NN 178.9 vs 11.0, Backprop 46.9 vs 20.7, K-means 1597.7 vs 572.2, Myocyte 2733.6 vs 555.4 (CUDA reference), Pathfinder 18.4 vs 7.4, SRAD 19.9 vs 16.1, MRI-Q 20.2 vs 15.5, OptionPricing 136.0 vs 106.8; slower: CFD 1878.2 vs 2235.9, HotSpot 35.9 vs 45.3, LavaMD 5.1 vs 6.7, LocVolCalib 1211.1 vs 1293.2. Artifact W8100 speedup files: srad 5.60, nn 5.14, hotspot 3.58, backprop 3.21, pathfinder 2.77, lavaMD 1.25, mri-q 1.24, OptionPricing 1.19, cfd 0.86, kmeans 0.79, LocVolCalib 0.62.
corrections.baseline: Hand-written OpenCL reference implementations from Rodinia 3.1 (CUDA for Myocyte on NVIDIA), Parboil 2.5 (MRI-Q) and FinPar (LocVolCalib, OptionPricing); the four Accelerate benchmarks (Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body) were compared against Accelerate 0.15.1 (a Haskell DSL with a CUDA backend), not C/C++.
corrections.workload: 16 GPU benchmarks manually translated to Futhark (Rodinia Backprop, CFD, HotSpot, K-means, LavaMD, Myocyte, NN, Pathfinder, SRAD; FinPar LocVolCalib, OptionPricing; Parboil MRI-Q; Accelerate Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body), datasets in the paper's Table 2; runtime averaged over 10 runs, excluding input upload, result readback and OpenCL context creation and kernel build on both sides (Rodinia timing patched to match).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Futhark compiler git 78c956ba58057ca6773cefb466efef2fa65c1386 with the OpenCL backend and no benchmark-specific flags; references built by their own suite Makefiles with gcc/g++ (-lOpenCL) and nvcc (CUDA 8.0 on NVIDIA). The paper and artifact state no host compiler versions or optimisation flags; Rodinia OpenCL Makefiles in the yuhc/gpu-rodinia mirror use g++ -g -O2 (backprop) and -g -O3 (nn). GPU kernels on both sides are compiled by the vendor OpenCL driver.
corrections.hardware: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 780 Ti with CUDA 8.0 and AMD FirePro W8100 (OpenCL benchmarks only); host CPU not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars, 210 forks; futhark-benchmarks 48 stars; futhark-pldi17 artifact 8 stars
corrections.caveats: The wins are mostly not a language-level effect: the paper attributes them to the hand-written references leaving work unoptimised, namely Rodinia NN leaving 100 reduce operations sequential on the CPU, Backprop leaving a reduction sequential, K-means not parallelising the cluster-centre update, and Myocyte/MRI-Q lacking coalescing or locality optimisation; the authors say the 0.79x geometric mean on the 4 slower benchmarks is 'a better estimation of where Futhark stands in relation to hand-optimised GPU code'. HotSpot and Pathfinder references use time tiling that Futhark lacks. Same benchmarks but different parallelisation strategies, so same_algorithm is false for the large speedups (NN 16x, Backprop, K-means, Myocyte). Accelerate rows compare against a Haskell DSL, not C. Timings exclude transfer and kernel build on both sides. Numbers are from 2017 Futhark on 2013-2014 GPUs; the C and multicore CPU backends are not compared against C here, and futhark-benchmarks itself publishes no results. futhark-website performance.md compares against Thrust and Rodinia HotSpot only as graphs, without numbers or hardware in the text. A 2026 arXiv snippet (seen only by the search agent) reports big-integer multiplication about 1.35x slower than hand-coded CUDA. Paper PDF: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diku-dk/futhark-website/HEAD/publications/pldi17.pdf.
corrections.why_faster: Compiler transformations that the hand-written references lack: Futhark parallelises reductions that Rodinia leaves sequential or on the CPU (NN, Backprop, K-means segmented reduction), applies automatic memory coalescing (K-means x9.26, Myocyte x4.2, OptionPricing x8.79, LocVolCalib x8.4), fusion (LavaMD x4.55, Crystal x10.1) and loop tiling (LavaMD, MRI-Q, N-body), and uses in-place updates. Its slowdowns come from unnecessary copying (HotSpot double buffering by copy, about 30% of runtime) and missing micro-optimisations. Both sides emit OpenCL C kernels compiled by the same vendor driver, so the gain comes from compiler-driven restructuring, not from a faster language runtime.

notes: Tier upgraded from D to B: the PLDI 2017 paper and its artifact were reachable via GitHub (futhark-website/publications/pldi17.pdf; diku-dk/futhark-pldi17 paper_data/aux_runtimes matches the paper's W8100 column). Main shortcoming for the orchestrator: the large speedups come from under-optimised Rodinia references (sequential CPU reductions in NN and Backprop, an unparallelised K-means update), and the authors themselves estimate 0.79x against hand-optimised GPU code, so same_algorithm is false and this is not a language win; consider whether the NN and Backprop rows fall under the crippled-baseline precedent.
